design.quote: A cross‑sectional surveillance study design was used to examine lifetime and past year misuse of oral tramadol and comparators of interest among NSHUH respondents aged 12 years or older.
design.text: Cross‑sectional surveillance study of US residents aged 12+ using NSDUH data

findings.quote: Tramadol is a centrally acting opioid analgesic with two mechanisms of action including weak activation of the µ opioid receptor by the parent drug, more potent activation by its primary metabolite (M1), and inhibition of the reuptake of serotonin and norepinephrine.
findings.text: Tramadol is a centrally acting opioid analgesic that weakly activates µ opioid receptors, more potently after conversion to metabolite M1, and also blocks serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake.

findings.where: Results › Oral tramadol versus alprazolam › 2012 to 2014 (Any lifetime misuse)
findings.quote: any lifetime misuse of oral tramadol increased from approximately 0.4% to 1.5% from 2002 through 2014.
findings.text: In the US survey, lifetime misuse of oral tramadol rose from about 0.4% to 1.5% between 2002 and 2014.

limits.where: Results › Data on misuse via injection
limits.quote: The NSDUH data included too few reports of tramadol use by injection to allow for reliable estimates or statistical comparisons with other drugs.
limits.text: The study could not provide reliable estimates of tramadol injection misuse because too few reports were available.

ref.title: Tramadol use and risk of seizure: A report of two cases and a review of recent literature

sources.title: Tramadol use and risk of seizure: A report of two cases and a review of recent literature
money: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.

design.quote: We identified two cases of seizures directly related to tramadol exposure. We then reviewed recent literature on tramadol and its adverse effects, particularly looking at its effect on seizure risk and the incidence of seizures.
design.text: Case report of two patients plus literature review of tramadol adverse effects

findings.where: Literature review › Tramadol pharmacology and analgesic effects
findings.quote: Seizures in particular are more common with tramadol than with other opioids, and can occur at therapeutic doses.
findings.text: Tramadol causes seizures more often than other opioids and they can happen at therapeutic doses.

findings.where: Literature review › Tramadol pharmacology and analgesic effects
findings.quote: Tramadol monotherapy has been reported to cause serotonin syndrome without concomitant serotonergic medications at high doses, but is more likely to occur when combined with other serotonergic agents.
findings.text: Tramadol can cause serotonin syndrome, especially when taken with other serotonergic medications.

findings.where: Literature review › Clinical reports and case series
findings.quote: patients prescribed tricyclic antidepressants and SSRI’s were 5–9.4 times more likely to experience seizures compared to patients not prescribed antidepressants.
findings.text: People who use tramadol together with tricyclic antidepressants or SSRIs are 5–9.4 times more likely to have seizures.
findings.second_hand: Another case-control study assessing the seizure risk in 11,383 patients exposed to tramadol reported that patients prescribed tricyclic antidepressants and SSRI's were 5-9.

limits.quote: We found that there were scarce recent studies on the relationship between tramadol and seizure risk.
limits.text: There are few recent studies on tramadol’s seizure risk.

findings.where: Mixing tramadol with other drugs / Physical health risks
findings.quote: Tramadol can depress breathing and may be risky for people with asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Tramadol use has been linked with serotonin syndrome. This is a potentially life‑threatening condition where the serotonin receptors are overstimulated.
findings.text: Tramadol can depress breathing, be risky for people with asthma or COPD, and has been linked with serotonin syndrome, a potentially life‑threatening condition.

findings.where: Mixing tramadol with other drugs / Mental health risks
findings.quote: If you are on certain antidepressants you should only take tramadol with clear medical advice because of the known risks.
findings.text: If people are on certain antidepressants, they should only take tramadol with clear medical advice because of the known risks.

findings.where: Mixing tramadol with other drugs / Can you get addicted?
findings.quote: Yes, tramadol is addictive. Over time, tramadol can produce cravings and a psychological desire to keep on using. Some people get addicted to tramadol after being prescribed it to treat a physical pain.
findings.text: Tramadol is addictive; over time it can produce cravings and a psychological desire to keep using, and some people become addicted after being prescribed it for physical pain.

limits.where: Mixing tramadol with other drugs / What is tramadol cut with?
limits.quote: If you’re not sure where the tablets have come from, there’s no way of knowing what’s inside them. Even testing kits may not find everything.
limits.text: If the source of tramadol tablets is unknown, there is no way of knowing what is inside them, and testing kits may not find everything.
